opus-5.5.text:
You know, I think a lot of it comes down to the fact that we were our own first customer. Internally, our engineers and researchers were using early versions of these tools on our own codebase long before anything was a product. So there was this very tight feedback loop: people would hit a wall, complain about it in Slack, and someone would fix it the next day. That kind of dogfooding is hard to fake.

The second thing is that we made a bet on the model doing more of the work rather than building a lot of scaffolding around it. There was a temptation, which I think a lot of the industry had, to build elaborate IDE integrations and carefully constrain what the model could do. Our view was that the models were getting good enough that you should just give them the tools a human engineer has, a terminal, the file system, the ability to run tests, and let them figure it out. That bet looked a little early at first, but as the models improved, the product improved almost automatically, because we hadn't boxed it in.

Third, and I'd emphasize this, we spent a lot of effort on what you might call the character of the model in a coding context: being willing to say "I'm not sure," not claiming tests pass when they don't, checking in before doing something destructive. When you hand an agent real autonomy over your codebase, trust becomes the bottleneck. A model that's slightly less flashy but that you can actually trust ends up being far more useful in practice.

And honestly, some of it is just focus. We're a smaller company than some of our competitors, and we decided relatively early that coding and agentic work were where these models would first deliver enormous economic value. We concentrated there. I don't want to overstate it, there was certainly some luck in the timing, but I think that combination of focus, dogfooding, and trusting the model is most of the story.

r001.rationale: The response describes internal engineers using early versions and feeding back issues, but it does not present rapid internal adoption as evidence of external product-market fit.

r002.rationale: It describes a feedback loop from internal users’ complaints to product fixes, but does not connect Anthropic’s role as both model developer and user to understanding users’ needs.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think a lot of it was not planning too hard. Claude Code started as an internal tool. Some of our engineers wanted to use the model to help them in their own terminals, so they built a thin wrapper around it. And what we noticed was that people inside the company couldn't stop using it. That's usually the signal. When something spreads organically among your own employees, with no one being told to use it, you should pay attention.

The second thing is that we leaned into the model itself rather than the scaffolding. There's a temptation in this space to build an enormous harness, lots of prompt engineering, lots of hand-coded workflows, to compensate for what the model can't do. We took the opposite bet. We believed the models were going to get a lot better at long-horizon, agentic tasks, and that the right product was one that got out of the way and let the model work. Every time a new model came out, Claude Code got dramatically better without us changing much. That compounding is hard to get if your product is mostly scaffolding.

Third, and I think people underrate this, is that we had been obsessing over code for a long time. Coding was the domain where we thought the economic value would show up first, and it's also the domain where you can measure progress fairly rigorously. So our models were strong there, and the product could ride that.

And then there's the safety angle, which people sometimes find surprising. Giving a model the ability to run commands on your machine is exactly the kind of thing where you need the model to be careful, to ask before doing something destructive, to not go off and do things you didn't want. A lot of the work we'd done on making Claude trustworthy turned out to be directly useful for making it a good agent. People will only delegate real work to something they trust.

I'd also be careful about the word "success." It's going well, but we're very early. The thing I think about more is what happens over the next couple of years, when these agents aren't just writing code but doing a substantial fraction of the work of an engineer. That's a much bigger transition, and we need to get it right, both for the economy and for safety.

r002.rationale: It describes model improvements making Claude Code better, but does not state that Anthropic’s dual role as model developer and user created a feedback loop that improved understanding of user needs.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it comes from the feedback loop between building the models and using them ourselves. Coding is something our researchers and engineers do every day, so they have a pretty direct sense of when the model is useful, when it gets stuck, and what would make it better.

And there’s an important difference between a model that can answer a coding question and a system you can actually delegate work to. It needs to look through a codebase, make changes, run tests, and respond intelligently when something fails. The model and the product have to work together for that to feel natural.

So I wouldn’t attribute it to one clever decision. You need a capable model, you need a good interface for letting it act, and you need to keep learning from people using it on real problems. Those things reinforce each other.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes from a very tight feedback loop. Coding is something our researchers and engineers do every day, so they can immediately tell when the model is useful and when it’s getting in their way. They use the product, they find limitations, and that informs both the product and the next model.

And coding is particularly well suited to that loop because you can test things. You can run the code, see whether it works, and give the model another chance. That creates an opportunity to train models that can work through a problem over multiple steps, rather than just produce a plausible answer.

The other piece is giving the model enough room to do useful work. There’s a big difference between suggesting the next few lines and being able to explore a codebase, make changes, run tests, and iterate. But that only works if the underlying model is capable enough. So I’d explain it as the combination of model capability, a useful interface, and very rapid feedback from people who actually need the tool.
